clue.text: Leaders, the best on hand

parts.note: the best of anything is the top
bananas grow in bunches called hands, so they are what you find on a hand

explanation.surface: The leading figures are the best people to have available when needed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On hand' looks like 'available', but read literally it means the fruit that grows on a hand: a bunch of bananas is called a hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Top bananas is an informal idiom for the most important people in a group or organisation.

clue.text: Catch Republican wearing listening device

indicators.note: the bugging device has the party letter on it like a garment, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: a tap is a device fitted to a phone line to eavesdrop

explanation.surface: A US politician gets caught out because he is carrying a hidden bug.
explanation.definitionFit: A snare or trick that catches someone out is a trap; the noun senses match.

clue.text: Encourage one in charge of meeting to provide transport for young

parts.note: to push someone is to urge or encourage them
the person who runs a meeting is its chair

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to take charge of a meeting so that children's transport can be arranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A baby buggy or stroller carries infants about, so it is a vehicle for the very young.

clue.text: Following behind, Queen!

parts.note: aft is the nautical word for at the back of a ship
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword abbreviation for the Queen

explanation.surface: Someone calls to the Queen to follow along behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' and 'behind' look like a pair of synonyms; only 'Following' defines, while 'behind' gives the ship's stern word.
explanation.definitionFit: Coming later in time or position is the sense shared, as in 'the day following'.

clue.text: Severe wind either side of Eunice

parts.note: Auster is the Roman name for the south wind

indicators.note: Eunice begins and ends with the same letter, so either side of the name gives that one letter

explanation.surface: A harsh gale blows round Storm Eunice, which hit Britain in 2022.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Either side' suggests two letters wrapped round something, but both ends of Eunice are E, so either side supplies just one E.
explanation.definitionFit: Austere and severe are synonyms for stern, strict or plain without ornament.

clue.text: Hermit's a powerless non-believer

indicators.note: without power, so P, the physics symbol for power, is dropped from the doubter

parts.note: a sceptic doubts or disbelieves

explanation.surface: A recluse is described as a doubter with no influence.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who lives in solitary self-denial, such as a desert monk, is an example of this.

clue.text: Break spell

definitions.meaning: to break suddenly, as a twig does
a short period, as in a cold spell of weather

explanation.surface: A magician tries to break an enchantment.
explanation.definitionFit: A brief period of weather, as in a cold snap, and a sudden crack both share the word.

clue.text: Relative, European, seen in French city

indicators.note: the European letter is seen inside the city's name

parts.note: Nice is a city on the French Riviera

explanation.surface: A European relative has been spotted in a French city.
explanation.definitionFit: A brother's or sister's daughter is a family member, so she is a relation.

clue.text: Things crossword compilers might assume?

parts.note: to assume here is to take on, as one adopts a name; setters publish under invented names

explanation.surface: A question about what setters might take for granted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Assume' suggests supposing; the cryptic sense is adopting, as one assumes a name. Telegraph and other setters write under assumed names.
explanation.definitionFit: Noms de plume adopted by writers to hide their real identity are what is meant.

clue.text: Property with a second TV

parts.note: a television is a TV set

explanation.surface: A house comes with a spare television.
explanation.definitionFit: Something valuable that a person owns counts as one of their possessions.

clue.text: Almost dismiss anger, say, about outrage

indicators.note: almost the whole word, so its final letter is cut

parts.note: to sack someone is to dismiss them from a job
to rile is to anger

indicators.note: turned about, so the abbreviation is read backwards

parts.note: e.g., for example, is what 'say' means here

explanation.surface: Someone nearly fires a person, or angers them, over a scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' cuts SACK to SAC, and 'about' turns the example abbreviation round; 'say' is not a homophone signal here.
explanation.definitionFit: Desecration of something holy is an outrage, a gross violation of what is revered.

clue.text: Losing head, Dietrich dancing is more irritating

indicators.note: the remaining letters dance into a new order
the first letter of the name is dropped

explanation.surface: Marlene Dietrich gets more irritated as she dances.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that makes you want to scratch more is more irritating; the comparative forms match.

clue.text: Proper business ruined, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a word spoken aloud and spelt differently

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, a business; wrecked means ruined

explanation.surface: A respectable firm is said to have been ruined.
explanation.definitionFit: Proper and right are synonyms for behaviour that follows the rules.

clue.text: Faith shown by mediocre editor

indicators.note: the letters are on show inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A mediocre editor displays religious belief.
explanation.definitionFit: A creed is a set of religious beliefs, so it is a faith.

clue.text: Suits could be this long to cover skin with diamonds

indicators.note: the yearning word covers the peeling word by going round it

parts.note: to long for is to pine
to strip is to skin or peel
D is the card abbreviation for diamonds

explanation.surface: Someone longs to cover their skin in diamonds while wearing suits.
explanation.definitionFit: Business suits are often patterned with thin vertical lines, so a suit can be this.

clue.text: Think of one publication in Spain

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
a mag is short for magazine, a publication
E is the international vehicle code for Spain

explanation.surface: Picture a single magazine published in Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: To picture or conceive something mentally is to think of it.

clue.text: Gather small number will make fire

parts.note: to gather in the sense of conclude is to infer
NO is the short form of number

explanation.surface: Collecting a few logs will be enough to make a fire.
explanation.definitionFit: A raging blaze, or hell itself, is an inferno; Italian for hell.

clue.text: The compiler's held in scorn, turning red

indicators.note: the setter's words are held inside the letters of the jumbled word
the letters of scorn are turned into a new order

parts.note: the compiler says 'I am', contracted to I'm

explanation.surface: The setter, mocked with contempt, is blushing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' rearranges SCORN into CRSON, which holds IM.
explanation.definitionFit: A deep blood colour is a shade of red.

clue.text: Sons outside remove illegal travellers

indicators.note: the two letters for sons sit outside the rest

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son, so sons gives two of them
to tow away a car is to remove it

explanation.surface: Boys standing outside get rid of people travelling without permission.
explanation.definitionFit: People who hide aboard a ship or plane to travel without paying travel unlawfully.

clue.text: People who don't wash the backs of their necks?

definitions.text: People who don't wash the backs of their necks?

parts.words: People who don't wash the backs of their necks?
parts.note: the scruff of the neck is its back, and untidy people are also called this

explanation.surface: A question about grubby people who miss a spot when washing.
explanation.walkthrough: The scruff is the nape of the neck; unwashed ones would be untidy, a pun on the noun for scruffy people.
explanation.definitionFit: Untidy, unkempt people are called by this informal British noun.

clue.text: For fans, fantastic plant

indicators.note: fantastic means wild and fanciful, so the letters are put into a wild new order

explanation.surface: For admirers, this is a marvellous plant.
explanation.definitionFit: The crocus that gives the spice is a flowering plant.

clue.text: A class act

parts.note: a, as in 'a day', means per
a school class is a form

explanation.surface: Someone praises a stage turn as first-rate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A class act' reads as praise for a performer; 'A' is per, 'class' is a school form, and 'act' is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To act on stage is to put on a show, the same verb sense.

clue.text: Supply press release with cycling video

parts.note: PR, public relations, is the business of press releases

indicators.note: the letters of video are cycled, the last one brought round to the front

explanation.surface: A press release is issued along with a video of cycling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cycling' moves the final O of VIDEO to the front, making OVIDE.
explanation.definitionFit: To furnish or hand over what is needed is to supply it.

clue.text: Maybe one in eight gallons ignored by farmer?

indicators.note: the letter for gallons is left out of the word

parts.note: a farmer is a grower of crops

explanation.surface: A farmer pays no attention to eight gallons of something.
explanation.walkthrough: An eight is a racing boat with eight oarsmen, so one in an eight is an oarsman; 'eight gallons' is a false pairing.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of a rowing eight crew is an example of an oarsman.

clue.text: Medical Officer leaving hospital is amusing

indicators.note: the hospital letter leaves the name

parts.note: Sir Chris Whitty is England's Chief Medical Officer

explanation.surface: A doctor going off duty at the hospital is entertaining.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Medical Officer' looks like MO, but it is Chris Whitty, England's Chief Medical Officer, prominent during the Covid pandemic.
explanation.definitionFit: Clever and funny in speech means amusing.

clue.text: Flowery area, part of America

parts.note: florid means elaborately flowery in style

explanation.surface: A region of the United States full of flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a US state, the Sunshine State in the south-east.

clue.text: Perfect view over lake

indicators.note: in a down clue the opinion word goes over, above, the lake letter

parts.note: a view or opinion is an idea

explanation.surface: An ideal view looks out over a lake.
explanation.definitionFit: Ideal and perfect are synonyms for something that could not be better.

clue.text: Boss cut short research

indicators.note: the word is cut short, losing its final letter

parts.note: to research a topic is to study it

explanation.surface: The manager has cut the research budget.
explanation.definitionFit: A boss is a raised knob or ornamental stud, as on a shield.

clue.text: Vessel with leak, right one for stew

parts.note: a pot is a vessel
to leak heavily is to pour out
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A cooking pot that leaks is the right one for making stew.
explanation.definitionFit: The word originally meant a stew of mixed meats, before it came to mean scented petals.

clue.text: Bang on, seeing former partner in front of a court

indicators.note: the old partner comes first, ahead of the rest

parts.note: an ex is a former spouse or partner

explanation.surface: It is right to see your ex standing before a court.
explanation.definitionFit: Bang on is British slang for precisely correct.

clue.text: Shock broadcast for Times

indicators.note: broadcast means spoken on air, so the word is heard rather than read

parts.note: to daze is to stun or shock

explanation.surface: A shock is broadcast for a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' looks like the London newspaper; it means periods, as in olden days.
explanation.definitionFit: Periods of history, as in 'in my day' or 'hard times', are meant.

clue.text: New dealer in US not yet met

indicators.note: new means made afresh, so these letters are made into a new order

explanation.surface: A newly arrived trader in America has not met anyone yet.
explanation.definitionFit: Hopes or ambitions not yet fulfilled are unachieved, as targets not met.
